docs.title: Wong Kin Chong O/A level Notes
docs.text: Welcome to my notes website. I am Kin Chong, currently studying Computer Science in NUS. On the side, I give tuition for O level and A level students on math and sciences.

docs.title: What's this website for
docs.text:
This website is created to support my students in their revision and independent learning. It provides an alternative set of notes for those who may find school materials insufficient or difficult to follow.

At the same time, I believe that education should be accessible to everyone. Not all students can afford tuition, so this platform is open to anyone who wishes to learn, revise, and improve at their own pace.

In the future, I hope to expand this website to include more features, such as a discussion forum, progress tracking, quizzes, and interactive visualisations. However, with current academic commitments, development may take some time. Thank you for your patience and support.

docs.title: Physical Quantities
docs.text:
Definition

Physical quantities are quantities that can be measured. They consist of a numerical magnitude and an unit.

docs.title: Base Quantites and their SI Units
docs.text:
A base quantity is a basic physical quantity that is defined independently while a derived quantity is formed by combining base quantites using a formula.

Base Quantity SI Base Unit Name Symbol Name Symbol Mass \(m\) kilogram kg Length \(l\) metre m Time \(t\) second s Electric current \(I\) ampere A Thermodynamic temperature \(T\) kelvin K Amount of substance \(n\) mole mol

docs.title: Derived Units
docs.text:
The units of derived quantities can be expressed in terms of base units using their defining formulae.

\[ Speed = \frac{distance}{time} \]
  • The SI unit of distance is \(m\) while the SI unit of time is \(s\)
  • Based on the formula, the unit of the derived quantity speed is \(m/s\)

docs.title: Homogenity of Physical Equations
docs.text: Physical quantities can only be added, subtracted or equated if they have the same units.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
Definition

Accuracy is the closeness of agreement between a measured value and a true value.

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
Definition

Precision is the degree of consistency and agreement among independent measurements of the same quantity.

docs.title: Random Errors
docs.text:
Definition

Random errors are deviations of the measured value from the mean value, with varying sings and magnitudes.

To reduce random errors

  1. Improve the procedure to minimize uncertainty due to random errors. (eg. Measure time taken for 20 oscillation and calculate period instead of measuring one period)
  2. Use a large sample size for the mean value to be a good estimate of the true value.

docs.title: Systematic Errors
docs.text:
Definition

Systematic errors are deviations of the mean value from the true value, with the same sign and similar magnitude

To reduce systematic errors

  1. Zero/Tare/Calibrate the apparatus

docs.title: Comparison of Random and Systematic Errors
docs.text: Type of error Characteristics If this error exists, will precision be affected? If this error exists, will accuracy be affected? random        varying in both magnitude and direction about a mean value, can be reduced       by taking average of repeated readings, but not eliminated.      Yes No systematic        varying in fixed direction about a true value, CANNOT be reduced by taking       average of repeated readings, but may be eliminated by good experimental       techniques.      No Yes

docs.title: Uncertainties
docs.text:
A measurement of a physical quantity X is reported in the form, X = (x \(\pm\) \(\Delta\) x) where \(\Delta\) x refers to the uncertainty associated with the measurement of X.

Definition

The fractional uncertainty is the ratio of the actual uncertainty to the measured value.

\[ \frac{\Delta x}{x} \]

Definition

The percentage uncertainty is obtained by converting the fractional uncertainty into percentage form.

\[ \frac{\Delta x}{x} \times 100\% \]

docs.title: Significant Figures and Decimal Places
docs.text:
1. Express uncertainties to 1 s.f
  2. Express the quantity to the same place value as its uncertainty.

docs.title: Adding or Subtracting
docs.text:
• For \(c = a + b\), the actual uncertainty in \(c\), \(\Delta c = \Delta a + \Delta b\)
  • For \(d = a - b\), the actual uncertainty in \(d\), \(\Delta d = \Delta a + \Delta b\)

docs.title: Multiplying or Dividing Measured Quantities
docs.text:
• For \(p = ab\), the fractional uncertainty in \(p\), \(\frac{\Delta p}{p} = \frac{\Delta a}{a} + \frac{\Delta b}{b}\)

  • For \(q = \frac{a}{b}\), the fractional uncertainty in \(q\), \(\frac{\Delta q}{q} = \frac{\Delta a}{a} + \frac{\Delta b}{b}\)

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: • If \(r = ka\), then \(\Delta r = k(\Delta a)\), where \(k\) is a constant.

docs.title: Powers
docs.text: • If \(s = a^n\), then \(\frac{\Delta s}{s} = |n| \frac{\Delta a}{a}\)

docs.title: Complicated Equations
docs.text:
Actual uncertainty of \(X\)

\[ \Delta X = \frac{1}{2}(\text{maximum possible } X - \text{minimum possible } X) \] \[ \Delta X = \frac{1}{2}(X_{\max} - X_{\min}) \]

docs.title: Scalars and Vectors
docs.text:
Definition"

Scalar quantities are physical quantities that have only magnitudes.

Definition"

Vector quantities are physical quantities that have both magnitudes and directions.

docs.title: Combining 1D Vectors
docs.text:
In 1D, there are only 2 directions. Therefore, we can choose one to be positive and the other to be negative.

To combine 1D vectors

  1. State Sign Convention (decide which direction is positive and which is negative)
  2. Add the vectors together to obtain the resultant vector. (the sign of the resultant vector indicates the direction of it)

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
1. Resolve both vectors
  2. Combine the horizontal and the vertical components to find the resultant horizontal vertical components
  3. Use Pythagoras Theorem to determine the magnitude of the resultant vector
  4. Use \(tan^{-1}\) to determine the angle/direction

docs.title: Atoms and Subatomic Particles
docs.text:
Learning Outcomes 1(a) identify and describe protons, neutrons and electrons in terms of their relative charges and relative masses 1(c) describe the distribution of mass and charges within an atom 1(d) deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons present in both atoms and ions given proton and nucleon numbers (and charge)

An atom is the smallest component of an element having the chemical properties of the element.

All atoms are made of up the same three subatomic particles

  • eletrons
  • protons
  • neutrons

The protons and neutrons make up the nucleus of the atom. Thus they are also referred to as nucleons. The electrons are surrounding the nucleus.

docs.title: Relative Mass and Charge of Subatomic Particles
docs.text: property proton electron neutron relative charge +1 -1 0 relative mass 1 \(\frac{1}{1836}\) 1

docs.title: Distribution of Mass and Charge in an Atom
docs.text:
So far, we know that

  • The protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus
  • The electrons have negligible mass compared to the protons and neutrons
  • The protons are positively charged
  • The electrons are negatively charged
  • The neutrons are neutral

Therefore, we can say that 99% of the mass is concentrated in the nucleus. All the positive charges are in the nucleus and the negative charges are on the electrons.

docs.title: Nuclide Notation
docs.text:
\[^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}\]

The proton number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of each atom of an element.

In the atom, the number of electrons is also equal to the number of protons since atoms are neutral

The nucleon number (A), also called the mass number, is the total number of neutrons and protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element.

docs.title: Deflection of ions and charged particles in Electric Field
docs.text: Learning Outcome 1(b) deduce the behaviour of beams of protons, neutrons and electrons in an electric field

docs.title: Ions
docs.text:
A negative ion (anion) has more electrons than protons.

A positive ion (cation) has more protons than electrons.

docs.title: What happens when particles pass through electric field
docs.text:
Since like charges repel and unlike charges attract, negatively charged particles such as electrons will be attracted to the positive plate while positively charged particles such as protons will be attracted to the negative plate.

Neutron particles such as neutrons experience no attraction/repulsion and thus are not deflected.

However, if you have not realised, the proton and electron are deflected by different angles! More precise, angle of deflection of electron is greater than that of proton.

The reason is simple and requires a tiny bit of Physics.

Both the electron and proton carry charge of the same magnitude of 1. Thus they experience forces of the same magnitude!

Therefore, the one with a smaller mass will deflect by a larger angle (imagine if you push an elephant and a ball with the same force, the elephant won't move a inch and the ball will fly!).

Since we know that electrons have a relative mass is \(\frac{1}{1836}\) while that of protons is 1, the electrons will deflect by a much greater angle.

To summaries all this

\[ angle \propto \frac{charge}{mass} \]

docs.title: Isotopes
docs.text:
Learning Outcome 1(e) (ii)distinguish between isotopes on the basis of different numbers of neutrons present

Isotopes are atoms of an element that have the same proton number but different nucleon numbers (or same number of protons and different number of neutrons).

Isotopes of an element have the same electronic configuration and thus have similar chemical properties (undergo similar reactions).

They have different relative isotopic masses and thus different physical properties (density etc).

docs.title: Relative Masses
docs.text: Learning Outcomes 6(a) define the terms relative atomic, isotopic, molecular and formula mass 6(c) calculate the relative atomic mass of an element given the relative abundances of its isotopes

docs.title: Relative Atomic Mass
docs.text:
\[ Relative \; atomic \; mass, A_{r} = \; \frac{average \; mass \; of \; one \; atom \; of \; an \; element}{\frac{1}{12} \; \times \; the \; mass \; of \; one \; atom \; of \; ^{12}C} \]

The relative mass of atom of an element is the ratio of the average mass of one atom of the element to \(\frac{1}{12}\) times the mass of one atom of \(^{12}C\)

docs.title: Relative Isotopic Mass
docs.text:
\[ Relative \; isotopic \; mass, \; A_{r} \; = \; \frac{average \; mass \; of \; an \; isotope \; of \; an \; element}{\frac{1}{12} \; \times \; the \; mass \; of \; one \; atom \; of \; ^{12}C} \]

The relative mass of an isotope of an element is the ratio of the average mass of an isotope of the element to \(\frac{1}{12}\) times the mass of one atom of \(^{12}C\)

docs.title: Relative Abundance of Isotopes
docs.text:
The percentage of a particular isotope compared to the total number of atoms of that element in a mixture of isotopes is called the isotopic abundance or the relative abundance.

\[ Relative \, Atomic \, Mass, \, A_{r} \; = \; \sum (relative \; isotopic \; mass \; \times \; isotopic \; abundance) \]

docs.title: Transition Metal
docs.text:
Defintion

A transition metal is a d-block element that form one or more stable ions with a partially filled d subshell.

Important

Zn and Sc are d block elements but they are not transition metal.

  • Zn forms \(Zn^{2+}\) with a fully filled d subshell \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^{10}\)
  • Sc forms \(Sc^{3+}\) with a empty d subshell \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6\)

docs.title: Electronic Configuration of Atoms
docs.text:
So far, we have learned principal quantum shells, subshells and orbitals and their relationship in term of energy level.

Now we are going to learn how electrons are allocated to the orbitals. The allocation is governed by 3 rules/laws/princiles.

docs.title: 1: The Aufbau Principle
docs.text:
Electrons in their ground states occupy orbitals in order of energy levels.

The orbital with the lowest energy level is always filled first.

Generally, in an atom, energy level increases with principal quantum number, 1s < 2s < 3s < ...

In the same principal quantum shell, energy level of subshells increases in the order of s, p, d, f; so 4s < 4p < 4d < 4d < ...

In the same principal subshell, orbitals are degenerate, so 3px = 3py = 3pz.

Important

Take note that 3d is more energetic than 4s when they are both empty. Therefore 4s is filled first 3d.

docs.title: Working Example
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the electronic configuration of Carbon which has 6 electrons.

  1. We start from the subshell with the lowest energy level which is 1s. Since 1s can accomodate up to 2 electrons, we get \(1s^2\)
  2. Then we are left with 4 electrons to allocate, and the next subshell with the lowest energy level is 2s. Since 2s can accomodate up to 2 electrons, we get \(1s^2 \, 2s^2\)
  3. Finally, we are left with 2 electrons to allocate, and the next subshell with the lowest energy level is 2p. Since 2p can accomodate up to 6 elestrons, we obtain \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^2\)

docs.title: 2: Hund's Rule of Multiplicity
docs.text: When filling subshells that contain more than one orbital with the same energy, each orbital must be singly occupied before electrons are paired.

docs.title: Working Example
docs.text: Suppose we want to find the electronic configuration of Oxygen which has 8 electrons.

docs.title: Pauli Exclusion Principle
docs.text:
An orbital cannot hold more than two electrons and the two electrons in the same orbtital must be in opposite spins.

This is shown in electron-in-box diagram where the box represents orbital and the arrows represents electrons.

The direction of the arrow indicates the spin of the electron.

This is principle is demonstrated in the working example for Hund's Rule of Multiplicity.

docs.title: Cr
docs.text: The electronic configuration of Cr is \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^5 \, 4s^1\) (instead of \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^4 \, 4s^2\))

docs.title: Cu
docs.text: The electronic configuration of Cr is \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^10 \, 4s^1\) (instead of \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^9 \, 4s^2\))

docs.title: Cations
docs.text:
1. First write the electronic configuration of the atom
  2. Remove the number of electrons equal to the positive charge, starting from the highest energy subshell

Important

4s electrons are removed before 3d

docs.title: Working Example
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the electronic configuration of \(Fe^{2+}\)

  1. First we find the electronic configuration of Fe, \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^6 \, 4s^2\)
  2. Remove 2 (since the charge is 2+) electrons, starting from the highest energy subshell, \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6 \, 3s^2 \, 3p^6 \, 3d^6\)

docs.title: Anions
docs.text:
1. First write the electronic configuration of the atom
  2. Add the number of electrons equal to the negative charge, starting from the lowest energy available subshell

docs.title: Working Example
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the eletronic configuration of \(N^{-3}\)

  1. First we find the electronic configuration of N, \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^3\)
  2. Add 3 (since the charge is -3) electrons, starting from the lowest energy available subshell which is found to be 2p, so \(1s^2 \, 2s^2 \, 2p^6\)

docs.title: Principal Quantum Shells, Subshells and Orbitals
docs.text: Learning Outcomes 1(f) describe the number of the relative energies of the s, p and d orbitals for the principal quantum number 1, 2 and 3 and also the 4s and 4p orbitals

docs.title: Principal Quantum Shells
docs.text:
Previously in O level, we learn that electrons reside in electronic shells.

However, now we have levelled up to A level and we will call these shells as principal quantum shells.

Each principal quantum shell is assigned with a principal quantum number

As the principal quantum number increases, size, maximum number of electrons (\(2n^{2}\)), and energy level increases.

principal quantum number 1 2 3 4 maximum number of electrons (\(2n^{2}\)) 2 8 18 32

docs.title: Subshells
docs.text:
Tip

Think of principal quantum shells like different hotels of a particular chain. Subshells are the storeys in the hotels.

Each principal quantum shell can be divided into subshells. The number of subshells in a principal quantum shell is the same as its principal quantum number.

principal quantum number, n number of subshell types of subshells notation for subshells 1 1 s 1s 2 2 s, p 2s, 2p 3 3 s, p, d 3s, 3p, 3d 4 4 s, p, d, f 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f

In the same principal quantum shell, the energy level of subshells increases in the order of s < p < d < f.

For subshells in different principal quantum shells, subshells in quantum shells with higher principal quantum number have higher energy levels. That is 1s < 2s < 3s.

docs.title: Orbitals
docs.text:
An atomic orbital is the region of space with 90% probability of finding an electron.

  • Subshells have orbitals at the same energy level (degenerate) but different orientations in space.
  • Each orbital can contain up to 2 electrons.
subshell number of orbitals maximum number fo electrons in each subshell s 1 2 p 3 6 d 5 10 f 7 14

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: principal quantum number, n subshell number of orbitals maximum number of electrons in each principal quantum shell, \(2n^{2}\) 1 1s 1 2 2 2s  2p 1  3 8 3 3s  3p  3d 1  3  5 18 4 4s  4p  4d  4f 1  3  5  7 32

docs.title: Shapes of Orbitals
docs.text: Learning Outcomes 1(g) describe the shapes of s, p and d orbitals

docs.title: The s Orbital
docs.text:
Each s subshell only has one s orbital.

s orbitals are spherical in shape.

The size of s orbitals increase with the principal quantum number, 1s < 2s < 3s < ...

docs.title: The p Orbital
docs.text:
Each p subshell has three p orbitals.

The p orbital is dumb-bell in shape.

The three p orbitals in the same quantum shell are identical in size, shape and energy level (degenerate) but differ in their spatial orientation. The three p orbitals are named \(P_x, P_y, P_z\).

The size and energy level of p orbitals increase with the principal quantum number, so 2p < 3p < 4P <...

docs.title: The d Orbital
docs.text:
Each d subshell has five d orbitals.

The 5 d orbitals are degenerate.

The five d orbitals are named \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{xz}\), \(d_{yz}\), \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\).

docs.title: Ionisation Energy
docs.text:
Definition

First Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of unipositively charged gaseous ions.

\[ X_{(g)} \rightarrow X^{+}_{(g)} + e^- \]

Definition

The nth Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous ions with a charge of (n - 1)+ to form 1 mole of gaseous ions with charge of n+.

\[ X^{(n - 1)+}_{(g)} \rightarrow X^{n+}_{(g)} + e^- \]

docs.title: Factors affecting ionisation energy
docs.text:
• Number of quantum shells. The larger the number of quantum shells in an atom, the further the electron is from the nucleus and hence experiences weaker nuclear attraction and is easier to remove, thus the lower the ionisation energy.
  • Effective Nuclear Charge, \(Z_{eff}\). The higher the effective nuclear charge, the stronger the attrative forces between teh nucleus and the electrons to be removed, hence the greater the ionisation energy.

docs.title: Trend in the Successive Ionisation Energies of the Same Element
docs.text:
\[ IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3 < IE_4 < ... \]
  • As electrons are removed from an atom, the nuclear charge remains constant as number of protons remains constant.
  • However, the shielding effect is reduced as the number of electrons decreases.
  • Hence, effective nuclear charge increases and the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outmost electron becomes stronger
  • Thus, more energy is needed to overcome the stronger attraction and remove the electron.
  • IE increases.

docs.title: Application of Successive Ionisation Energies
docs.text:
Suppose we have the successive IE of an unknown atom, we can identify the group of this atom from the successive IE.

  • The first big increase is from \(2^{nd}\) to \(3^{rd}\) ionisation energies.
  • This is because the third electron is from an inner quantum shell.
  • Thus there are two electrons in the outermost value shell.
  • Therefore, this atom is from group 2.

Important

  • Generally, a large increase implies removal of an inner quantum shell electron.
  • A small increase implies removal of an inner subshell electron in the same quantum shell.

docs.title: Trend in the First Ionisation Energies Down the Group
docs.text:
Down the group

  • The nuclear charge increases as proton number increases
  • The shielding effective increases as number of inner electrons increases
  • Thus, effective nuclear charge remains relatively constant.
  • As the number of quantum shell increases, the electrostatic forces of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron is weaker.
  • Therefore, less energy is required to overcome the weaker attraction
  • As a result, the first ionisation energy decreases.

docs.title: Trend in the First Ionisation Energies Across Period 2
docs.text:
Across Period 2

  • The number of quantum shells remains constant
  • Nuclear charge increases as the number of protons increases
  • Shielding effect remains relatively constant as additional electron is added to the outermost quantum shell
  • Thus, effective nuclear charge increases and the electrostatic force of attraction between nucleus and outermost eletron is stronger
  • More energy is required to overcome the stronger attraction.
  • Therefore, the first ionisation energy increases across period 2 and 3.

There are two dip in first IE

  • From Group 2 to Group 3
  • From Group 15 to Group 16

docs.title: Dip from Group 2 to Group 3
docs.text:
Electronic Configuration of Group 2 atom: \(ns^2\)

Electronic Configuration of Group 3 atom: \(ns^2 \, np^1\)

  • The first IE of the group 2 atom involves the removal of s electron while the first IE of the group 3 atom involves the removal of p electron.
  • Since the p electron is further away from the nucleus than the s electron.
  • There is weaker attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron.
  • Hence less energy is required to remove the p electron, resulting in a lower ionisation energy.

docs.title: Dip from Group 15 to Group 16
docs.text:
Electronic Configuration of Group 15 atom: \(ns^2 \, np^3\)

Electronic Configuration of Group 16 atom: \(ns^2 \, np^4\)

  • All p electrons in the Group 15 atom are unpaired, two of p electrons in Group 16 are paired.
  • There is some inter-electronic repulsion between the paired electrons in the p subshell of the Group 16 atom.
  • Thus less energy is required to remove one of the pair electron from the Group 16 atom.

docs.title: Trend in the First Ionisation Energies Across Transition Elements
docs.text:
• The first IE involves removal of a 4s electron.
  • The nuclear charge increase due to increasing proton number across transition elements.
  • The shielding effect also increases as additional electron is added to the inner d subshell, thereby nullifying the influence of each additional proton.
  • Thus effective nuclear charge remains almost constant.
  • Since the number of quantum shells is constant, the energy required to remove the outermost electron remains largely invariant.

docs.title: Down the Group
docs.text:
Down the group

  • The nuclear charge increases as the proton number increases.
  • The shielding effect increases as the number of inner electrons increases.
  • Therefore the effective nuclear charge remains relatively constant.
  • As the number of principal quantum shells increases, the outermost electrons are further away from the nucleus.
  • Hence the atomic radius increases.

docs.title: Across Period 2 and 3
docs.text:
Across Period 2

  • The number of quantum shells remain constant across the period.
  • Nuclear charge increases as the proton number increases.
  • Shielding effect remain relatively constant as the electrons are added to the same outermost shell.
  • Effective nuclear charge increases, resulting in stronger electrostatic forces of attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron.
  • Outermost electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus and hence the atomic radius decreases.

docs.title: Across the first row of Transition Elements
docs.text:
Across the first row of transition elements

  • Number of quantum shells remains constant
  • Nuclear charge increases due to increasing number of electrons.
  • Electrons are added to the inner 3d subshell, which contributes to the shielding effect.
  • Thus shield effect increases, nullifying the increase in nuclear charge due to every additional proton.
  • The effective nuclear charge ramins almost constant.

docs.title: Down the Group
docs.text:
Down the group

  • The nuclear charge increases as proton number increases
  • The shielding effective increases as number of inner electrons increases
  • Thus, effective nuclear charge remains relatively constant.
  • As the number of quantum shell increases, ionic radius increases.

docs.title: Across Period 2 and 3
docs.text:
• The ions, \(Na^-\), \(Mg^{2+}\), \(Al^{3+}\) and \(Si^{4+}\) are said to be isoelectronic as they have the same number of electrons.
  • Similarly, \(P^{3-}\), \(S^{2-}\) and \(Cl^-\) are also isoelectronic.
  • Across both isoelectronic series, the number of quantum shells reamins constant.
  • The nuclear charge increases as the number of protons increases.
  • The shielding effect remains constant as the number of electrons remains constant.
  • Therefore, the effective nuclear charge increases, resulting in a stronger attraction between the outermost electrons and the nucleus.
  • Thus, the ionic radius decreases across both isoelectronic series

There is a sharp increase in ionic radius from the cation series to the anion series. This is because the anions have one more quantum shell than the cations.

docs.title: Number of Quantum Shells and Effective Nuclear Charge
docs.text:
Electrons are held in the atom by electrostatic force of attraction between the positively charged nucleus and negatively charged electrons.

The strength of this electrostatic force of attraction results in difference in

  • atomic radii
  • ionic radii
  • ionisation energies
  • electronegativity

Therefore, it is important for us to understand how this electrostatic force of attraction varies across different elements.

The two factors that affect this attraction are

  • Number of quantum shells
  • Effective Nuclear Charge, \(Z_{eff}\)

docs.title: Number of quantum shells
docs.text: The number of quantum shells determines how far the outermost electron is from the nucleus. The further the outermost electron is from the nucleus, the weaker the attraction between the outermost electron and the nuclues. (If you happen to take H2 Physics, this is verified by the equation for electric force \(F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\))

docs.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
docs.text:
The effective nuclear charge, \(Z_{eff}\), is the net nuclear charge experienced by an outer electron. \(Z_{eff}\) depends on

  • Nuclear Charge (Z): The nuclear charge is dependent on the number of protons. The larger the number of protons, the greater the nuclear charge and the attraction for the outermost electrons by the nucleus.
  • Shielding Effect(S): Presence of inner shell electrons reduces the electrostatic attraction between the outermost electrons and the nucleus.
\[ Z_{eff} = Z - S \]

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text: Learning Outcome 2(a) show understanding that all chemical bonds are electrostatic in nature and describe:  (i) ionic bond as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions  (ii) covalent bond as the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and positively charged nuclei  (iii) metallic bond as the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalized electrons 2(b) describe, including the use of dot-and-cross diagrams:  (i) ionic bonding as in sodium chloride and magnesium oxide  (ii) covalent bonding as in hydrogen; oxygen; nitrogen; chlorine; hydrogen chloride; carbon dioxide; methane; ethene  (iii) co-ordinate (dative covalent) bonding, as in formation of the ammonium ion and in the \(Al_2Cl_6\) molecule 7(e) explain, in qualitative terms, the effect of ionic charge and of ionic radius on the numerical magnitude of a lattice energy (Refer to Topic 5 Chemical Energetics) 2(c) describe covalent bonding in terms of orbital overlap (limited to s and p orbitals only), giving \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) bonds 2(d) explain the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules such as \(BF_3\) (trigonal planar); \(CO_2\) (linear); \(CH_4\) (tetrahedral); \(NH_3\) (trigonal pyramidal); \(H_2O\) (bent); \(SF_6\) (octahedral) by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory 2(e) predict the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules analogous to those specified in (d) 2(f) explain and deduce bond polarity using the concept of electronegativity [quantitative treatment of electronegativity is not required] 2(g) deduce the polarity of a molecule using bond polarity and its molecular shape (analogous to those specified in (d)) 2(h) describe the following forces of attraction (electrostatic in nature):  (i) intermolecular forces, based on permanent and induced dipoles, as in \(CHCl_3(l)\); \(Br_2(l)\) and the liquid noble gases  (ii) hydrogen bonding, using ammonia and water as examples of molecules containing \(-NH\) and \(-OH\) groups 2(i) outline the importance of hydrogen bonding to the physical properties of substances, including ice and water 2(j) explain the terms bond energy and bond length for covalent bonds 2(k) compare the reactivities of covalent bonds in terms of bond energy, bond length and polarity 2(l) describe, in simple terms, the lattice structure of a crystalline solid which is:  (i) ionic, as in sodium chloride, magnesium oxide  (ii) simple molecular, as in iodine  (iii) giant molecular, as in graphite; diamond  (iv) hydrogen-bonded, as in ice  (v) metallic, as in copper  [the concept of the 'unit cell' is not required] 2(m) describe, interpret and/or predict the effect of different types of structure and bonding on the physical properties of substances 2(n) suggest the type of structure and bonding present in a substance from given information 5(b) describe and explain qualitatively the general trends and variations in atomic radius, ionic radius, first ionization energy and electronegativity,  (i) across a Period in terms of shielding and nuclear charge,  (ii) down a Group in terms of increasing number of electronic shells, shielding and nuclear charge  (Refer to Topic 1 Atomic Structure & Physical Periodicity for trends and variations in atomic and ionic radii, and first ionization energy.) 5(c) interpret the variation in melting point and in electrical conductivity across a Period in terms of structure and bonding in the elements (metallic, giant molecular, or simple molecular) (Refer to Topic 21 Chemical Periodicity) 5(d) describe and explain the trend in volatility of the Group 17 elements in terms of instantaneous dipole-induced dipole attraction (Refer to Topic 21 Chemical Periodicity) 11.1(d) describe \(sp^3\) hybridisation, as in ethane molecule, \(sp^2\) hybridisation, as in ethene and benzene molecules, and \(sp\) hybridisation, as in ethyne molecule (Refer to Topic 12 Arenes with regards to benzene) 11.1(e) explain the shapes of, and bond angles in, the ethane, ethene, benzene and ethyne molecules in relation to \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) carbon-carbon bonds (Refer to Topic 12 Arenes with regards to benzene)

docs.title: Electronegativity
docs.text:
Definition

Electronegativity of an atom is a measure of its ability to attract the electrons in a covalent bond to itself.

docs.title: Across the Period
docs.text:
• Number of quantum shells remains constant.
  • Nuclear charge increases while shielding effect remains relatively constant.
  • Effective Nuclear Charge increases across the period.
  • Thus electronegativity increases.

docs.title: Down the Group
docs.text:
• Nuclear charge and shielding effect both increases.
  • Effective nulear charge remains relatively constant
  • Number of quantum shell increases
  • Thus, electronegativity decreases

docs.title: ELectronegativity and Chemical Bonding
docs.text:
The difference in electronegativity between two atoms can be used to predict the type of bond between them.

\[ \text{similar electronegativity} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{electron sharing} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{covalent bonding} \] \[ \text{large difference in electronegativity} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{electron transfer} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{ionic bonding} \]

docs.title: Nature of Chemical Bonding
docs.text: All chemical bonding is electrostatic forces of attraction between positively charged and negatively charged particles.

docs.title: Giant Metallic Lattice Structure and Metallic Bonding
docs.text:
Metals in the solid state have a giant metallic lattice structure which is a lattice of metal cations and the sea of delocalised electrons held together by metallic bonding.

Metallic Bonding is the electrostatic force of attraction between the positively charged lattice of metal ions and the negatively charged sea of delocalised electrons.

docs.title: Factor 1: Number of valence electrons contributed per metal atom
docs.text: The larger the number of valence electrons contributed per atom, the greater the number of delocalised electrons, the stronger the metallic bonding.

docs.title: Factor 2: Charge and radius of the metal cation (Charge density)
docs.text: The higher the charge and the smaller the radius of the metal cation, the higher is charge density, and the stronger the metallic bonding.

docs.title: High melting and boiling points
docs.text:
• Boiling and Melting metals needs to overcome the metallic bonding
  • Metal has strong metallic bonding between the lattice of positive ions and the negatively charged sea of delocalised electrons.
  • Large amount of energy is required to overcome the strong metallic bonding.
  • Therefore, metals have high boiling and melting points.

Tip

To compare the boiling point and melting point of different metals

Compare the strength of their metallic bonding by comparing the 1. number of valence electrons contributed per metal atom and the 2. charge and redius of the metal cation.

The metal with stronger metallic bonding has a higher boiling and melting point.

docs.title: Good electrical and thermal conductivity
docs.text:
• Metal has a giant metallic lattice structure which consists of a lattice of positively charged ions and a negatively charged sea of delocalised electrons.
  • The delocalised electrons can act as mobile charge carriers to conduct electricity
  • The delocalised electrons also transfer heat quickly throughout the metal via conduction.

docs.title: Malleable and ductile
docs.text:
Malleable describes materials that can be hammered, pressed, or rolled into thin sheets without breaking

Ductile describes the ability to be stretched, bent or drawn into thin wires without breaking

  • When a strong enough force is applied, the layers of ions will slide over one another into new positions.
  • The shape of metal changes but it does not break because the sea of delocalised electrons prevent repulsion between the cations and the metallic bonding remains intact.

docs.title: Hardness
docs.text:
• Metals have strong metallic bonding between the lattice of positive ions and the negatively charged sea of delocalised electrons.
  • A strong force is required to overcome the strong metallic bonding.
  • Thus metals are hard.

docs.title: Giant Ionic Lattice Structure and Ionic Bonding
docs.text:
Ionic compounds in solid state have a giant ionic lattice structure which is lattice of cations and anions held together by ionic bonding.

Ionic Bonding is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

docs.title: Lattice Energy
docs.text:
Definition

Lattice energy is defined as the heat evolved when 1 mole of a pure ionic solid is formed from its constituent gaseous ions.

We use lattice energy to compare the strength of ionic bonding.

The larger the magnitude of lattice energy, the stronger the ionic bonding.

The magnitude of lattice energy depends on

  1. The charge of ions
  2. The radii of ions
\[ LE \propto \frac{q_+ \times q_-}{r_+ + r_-} \]

Tip

Ionic charge usually affects lattice energy more than ionic radius because the ionic charges are multiplied together in the numerator.

docs.title: High Boiling and Melting Points
docs.text:
• Ionic Compounds have giant ionic lattice structure with strong ionic bonding between the oppositely charged ions
  • Large amount of energy is required to overcome the strong ionic bonding to melt/boil them.
  • Thus, ionic compounds have high boiling and melting points.

docs.title: Good Electrical Conductivity in Molten and Aqueous State
docs.text:
• In molten / aqueous state, ionic compounds contain free moving ions which can act as mobile charge carriers
  • Therefore, molten and aqueous ionic compounds can conduct electricity.

Tip

The electrical conductivity of aqueous ionic compounds increases as concentration of ions increases.

docs.title: Hard but Brittle
docs.text:
Ionic compounds are Hard

  • Ionic Compounds have giant ionic lattice structure with strong ionic bonding between the oppositely charged ions
  • A strong force is required to overcome the strong ionic bonding.
  • Thus, ionic compounds are hard.

Ionic compounds are Brittle

  • When a large enough force is applied, the layers of ions are displaced.
  • Ions of like charges move closer to one another.
  • The repulsion between ions of like charges cause the lattice to shatter.
  • Thus, ionic compounds are brittle.

docs.title: Solubility
docs.text: Ionic Compounds are soluble in water but not in organic solvent

docs.title: Covalent Bonding
docs.text:
A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons.

Definition

Covalent bonding is the electrostatic force of attraction between the negatively charged shared electrons and the positively charged nuclei.

docs.title: Orbital Overlap
docs.text:
• In order for a covalent bond to be formed, the orbitals of the two atoms must overlap.
  • The shared electrons or bond pairs occupy the overlapping region.

docs.title: Sigma, \(\sigma\), bond
docs.text: • Sigma (\(\sigma\)) bond is formed by head-on overlap of two orbitals

docs.title: Pi, \(\pi\), bond
docs.text: • Pi (\(\pi\)) bond is formed by side-on overlap of two orbitals

docs.title: Sigma vs Pi bonds
docs.text: Pi bond is weaker than sigma bond as the degree of overlap is smaller in pi bond.

docs.title: Sigma and Pi bonds in Single, Double and Triple bonds
docs.text:
• A single bond consists of a \(\sigma\) bond
  • A double bond consists of a \(\sigma\) bond and a \(\pi\) bond
  • A double bond consists of a \(\sigma\) bond and two \(\pi\) bond

docs.title: Bond Energy
docs.text:
Definition

Bond energy is the average amount of energy required to break 1 mole of a covalent bond in the gaseous state to form gaseous atoms.

For example

\[ \mathrm{C-H}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{(g)} + \mathrm{H}_{(g)} \]

Bond energy is indicative of the strength of covalent bonds. The larger the bond energy, the stronger to covalent bond.

docs.title: Bond length
docs.text:
• Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of the two bonded atoms.
  • The shorter the bond length, the stronger the bond.
  • Smaller atoms form shorter and stronger bonds.

docs.title: Bond Order
docs.text:
• Bond order is the number of covalent bonds between a pair of atoms
  • Multiple bonds are shorter and strong than single bonds.
  • Triple bond > Double bond > Single bond

docs.title: Dot and Cross Diagram of Ionic Compounds
docs.text:
1. Draw the dot and cross diagrams of ions
  2. Make sure the number of ions is consistent with the formula

docs.title: Steps to Draw Dot and Cross Diagram for Covalent Molecules
docs.text:
1. Decide on the central atom. The central atom is usually the one with the lowest electronegativity or the one that can form more covalent bonds

  1. For polyatomic ions:

    • For each - charge, add one electron to the more electronegative atom.
    • For each + charge, remove one electron from the less electronegative atom

  2. Make terminal atoms achieve octet

  1. Check the central atom:
    • Elements from period 2 cannot expand octet. If there are more than 8 electrons, change a double bond to a dative bond
    • Elements from Period 3 onwards can expand octet.
    • Elements in Group 2 and 13 may be electron deficient
    • Element in Group 15 and 17 may have unpaired electrons

docs.title: Dative Bonding
docs.text:
A co-ordinate bond or dative bond between two atoms is a covelent bond in which both bonding electrons come from one atom.

  • To form a dative bond, the donor atom must have a lone pair
  • The acceptor atom must contain an empty orbital in its valence shell

Example \(\mathrm{NH_3BF_3}\)

Example \(\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}\)

Example \(\mathrm{NH^+_4}\)

docs.title: Electron Deficient Species
docs.text: Central atoms can have fewer than 8 electrons

docs.title: Expansion of Octet
docs.text:
• Elements from period 3 and onwards can form more than 4 bonds by using their d orbitals
  • We say they can expand its octet by using energetically accessible d orbitals

docs.title: Radical
docs.text:
• In some molecules, the central atoms have unpaired electrons
  • Species with unpaired electrons are called radical
  • Radicals are very reactive

docs.title: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion Theory
docs.text:
• The electrons pairs (or groups) around the central atom of a molecule (or ion) arrange themselves as far apart as possible so as to minimise their mutual repulsion.
  • The repulsion between lone pair and lone pair > lone pair and bond pair > bond pair and bond pair

docs.title: Hybridisation Theory
docs.text:
Let's look at the structure of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\)

The carbon atom forms 4 single bonds, one with each of the 4 hydrogen atoms.

Since there are 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pair, the shape w.r.t the carbon atom is tetrahedral and the bond angle is 109.5 degree.

Based on what we have learned so far, we can confidently deduce that these 4 single bonds consist of 1 s-s and 3 p-s \(\sigma\) bonds between the carbon atom and the 4 hydrogen atoms.

However, the s orbital and the three p orbitals of carbon are arranged in such a way that the p orbitals are perpendicular to one another, with angles of 90 degree between them. If that is the case, how can methane have a tetrahedral shape with bond angles of 109.5 degree?

Linus Pauling proposed that valence atomic orbitals of atoms in a molecule are different from those isolated atoms.

In the hybridisation theory, atomic orbitals (s and p in H2 chemistry) mix to form new orbitals called hybrid orbitals which can involve in \(\sigma\) bonding.

Hybridisation of orbitals results in hybrid orbitals with the same shape, size and energy level (degenerate)

docs.title: \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) Hybridisation
docs.text:
Let's look at \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) again

In \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), the carbon atom forms 4 \(\sigma\) bond and it has a tetrahedral shape.

Therefore, the carbon atom in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) is \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised

1 s and 3 p orbitals mix to form 4 \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybrid orbitals. These 4 hybrid orbitals are arranged in tetrahedral shape.

docs.title: \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) Hybridisation
docs.text:
Let's look at \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\)

In \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\), the carbon atom forms 3 \(\sigma\) bonds and 1 \(\pi\) bond and it has a shape of trigonal planar.

Since it needs to form a \(\pi\) bond, it needs to reserve 1 p orbital.

Thus it is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hydridised.

1 s and 2 p orbitals mix to form 3 \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybrid orbitals. These 3 hybrid orbitals are arranged in trigonal plannar shape and the unhybridised p orbital is perpendicular to the hybrid orbitals.

docs.title: \(\mathrm{sp}\) Hybridisation
docs.text:
Let's look at \(\mathrm{CO_2, CHN_3}\)

In both molecules, the carbon atom forms 2 \(\sigma\) bonds and 2 \(\pi\) bonds and the molecules are linear.

Since it needs to form 2 \(\pi\) bond, it needs to reserve 2 p orbital.

Thus it is \(\mathrm{sp}\) hydridised.

1 s and 1 p orbital mix to form 2 \(\mathrm{sp}\) hybrid orbitals. These 2 hybrid orbitals are arranged in linear shape and the unhybridised p orbitals are perpendicular to the hybrid orbitals.

docs.title: Hybridisation and strength of covalent bond
docs.text:
\(\mathrm{sp^3}\), \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) and \(\mathrm{sp}\) orbitals have different length/size due to different amount of p character.

\(\mathrm{sp^3}\) orbital is the longest / most elongated as \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) orbitals come from mixing 1 s and 3 p orbitals. \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) orbital (1 s and 2 p orbital) is the second most elongated and \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) orbital (1 s and 1 p orbital) is the least elongated.

Since bond length affects strength of covalent bonds, \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) orbital forms the weakest bond, followed by \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) and \(\mathrm{sp}\) orbitals

docs.title: Ionic Bonding with Covalent Character
docs.text:
In ideal ionic bonding, there is complete electron transfer.

The nucleus of the cation and that of the anion only attracts its own electrons.

However, the cation tends to attract electrons of anion causing the electron cloud of the anion to be polarised or distorted

docs.title: Factors thats affects Degree of Covalent Character
Polarising Power of Cation
docs.text:
• Cations with high charge density (small radius and high charge) have high polairsing power.
  • These cations have a higher tendency to distort the anions' electron cloud, resulting in greater covalent character in ionic bonding

docs.title: Polarisability of the anion
docs.text:
• Anions that are large (large number of electrons or larger radius) have high polarisability.
  • This is because their valence electrons are further from and less attracted by the nucleus.
  • Thus, the electron cloud is easily distorted by a cation, resulting in greater covalent character in the ionic bonding

docs.title: Bond Polarity
docs.text:
• In an covalent bond between two atoms of the same element, the electrons are equally shared as the atoms have the same electronegativity.

  • However, in an covalent bond between two atoms with different electronegativities, the electrons are pulled towards to more electronegative atom. The electrons are thus not equally shared. This bond is thus polar

  • This results in dipole on the bond and partial charges on the atoms

docs.title: Molecular Polarity
docs.text:
• Depending on the shape of the molecule, the individual dipoles may or may not cancel each other completely.
  • If the net dipole is 0, the molecule is non-polar, else it is polar
